set1.io: Compare and contrast ECG manifestations of electrolyte abnormalities.
set1.q: A 50-year-old woman has a long ST segment and long QTc. Her T wave is checked. What does it look like in hypocalcemia?
opts: Normal in shape and duration
Correct. Hypocalcemia prolongs the ST segment without affecting the duration of the T wave: a long QTc with a normally shaped T wave.
Tall, peaked and symmetric
Tall, peaked, symmetric T waves are hyperkalemia; in hypocalcemia the T wave stays normal.
Flattened with a U wave
A flattened T wave followed by a prominent U wave is hypokalemia; hypocalcemia keeps a normal T wave.
Pushed against the QRS
A T wave pushed against the QRS is hypercalcemia, from a shortened ST segment, the opposite of hypocalcemia.
set1.cite: 16. EKG Pericarditis Electrolytes and Other Abnormalities.pptx, Slide 40

set1.io: Topic — Preexcitation and accessory pathway tachycardias
set1.q: A 25-year-old woman has a preexcitation syndrome. Which is the most common one?
opts: Brugada syndrome
Brugada syndrome is an inherited sodium-channel disease of the right ventricular outflow tract, not a preexcitation syndrome.
Early repolarization
Benign early repolarization is a normal variant ST elevation, not an accessory pathway syndrome.
Wolff-Parkinson-White
Correct. The most common preexcitation syndrome is Wolff-Parkinson-White, in which the accessory pathway is the bundle of Kent.
Left bundle branch block
A left bundle branch block is delayed, not early, ventricular activation.
set1.cite: 16. EKG Pericarditis Electrolytes and Other Abnormalities.pptx, Slide 25

set1.io: Recognize ECG changes associated with: digoxin toxicity, amiodarone toxicity, tricyclic antidepressant toxicity
set1.q: A 23-year-old woman took an overdose of amitriptyline, a tricyclic antidepressant. Her 12-lead is shown. Which drug effect causes her fast heart rate?
opts: Beta-receptor blockade
Beta blockade slows the heart; it is one of amiodarone's actions, not the cause of tricyclic tachycardia.
Anticholinergic activity
Correct. Tricyclic antidepressants' anticholinergic activity causes the tachycardia; their fast sodium-channel blockade widens the QRS (the wide complexes on this tracing), and the QT is prolonged.
Sodium-potassium pump inhibition
Pump inhibition is digoxin's mechanism, with frequent premature ventricular complexes as its commonest result.
Raised serum calcium
High calcium shortens the ST segment and QTc; it is not what speeds the heart in a tricyclic overdose.
set1.cite: 16. EKG Pericarditis Electrolytes and Other Abnormalities.pptx, Slide 49
set1.alt: Twelve-lead electrocardiogram on grid paper, with each lead labeled

set1.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with: COPD/COLD, pulmonary embolism, hypothermia
set1.q: A 47-year-old woman with a pulmonary embolism has new ST-segment and T-wave changes. What causes them?
opts: Localized myocardial ischemia
Correct. In pulmonary embolism, localized myocardial ischemia leads to specific ST-segment and T-wave changes, alongside tachycardia and a rightward axis.
Pericardial inflammation
Pericardial inflammation gives global concave ST elevation with PR depression, not the embolism's ST-T changes.
An accessory pathway
An accessory pathway produces a short PR and delta wave, not ischemic ST-T changes.
Low serum calcium
Low calcium lengthens the ST segment; the embolism's ST-T changes come from localized ischemia.
set1.cite: 16. EKG Pericarditis Electrolytes and Other Abnormalities.pptx, Slide 50

set1.io: Topic — Preexcitation and accessory pathway tachycardias
set1.q: A 21-year-old man with preexcitation has a short PR interval. Why is it short?
opts: The sinoatrial node fires faster
The sinus rate does not set the PR interval; skipping the atrioventricular node's delay does.
The atria contract more slowly
Slower atrial contraction would not shorten the PR; bypassing the atrioventricular node does.
It bypasses the atrioventricular node
Correct. Because the accessory pathway bypasses the atrioventricular node, where the impulse is normally slowed, ventricular depolarization starts early and the PR interval is short.
The bundle branches are blocked
Bundle branch block widens the QRS without shortening the PR interval.
set1.cite: 16. EKG Pericarditis Electrolytes and Other Abnormalities.pptx, Slide 27

set1.io: Recognize ECG changes associated with: digoxin toxicity, amiodarone toxicity, tricyclic antidepressant toxicity
set1.q: An 86-year-old man taking digoxin develops toxicity although his dose is unchanged. Which explanation does the definition of toxicity allow?
opts: Digoxin blocks the bundle of Kent
The bundle of Kent is the Wolff-Parkinson-White accessory pathway; digoxin toxicity is buildup or oversensitivity.
His calcium has fallen too low
Low calcium lengthens the ST segment; it is not the definition of digoxin toxicity.
Toxicity needs a dose increase
Toxicity can occur without a higher dose, when the drug builds up or the heart becomes overly sensitive.
His heart has become overly sensitive
Correct. Digoxin toxicity occurs when too much digoxin builds up in the body or when the heart becomes overly sensitive to it.
set1.cite: 16. EKG Pericarditis Electrolytes and Other Abnormalities.pptx, Slide 47

set1.io: Compare and contrast ECG manifestations of electrolyte abnormalities.
set1.q: A 71-year-old woman with kidney failure has the 12-lead shown. Which finding on it is the early sign of her electrolyte disturbance?
opts: Flattened P waves
Flattened P waves are a hyperkalemia sign too, but they come later than the peaked T wave.
A wide QRS
QRS widening is a later hyperkalemia change, after the peaked T waves and P-wave flattening.
A sine wave
The sine wave is the last and most severe hyperkalemia pattern, not the early sign.
Peaked T waves
Correct. In hyperkalemia the peaked, symmetric T wave is the early sign; flattened P waves, a wide QRS and finally a sine wave follow as the potassium climbs.
set1.cite: 16. EKG Pericarditis Electrolytes and Other Abnormalities.pptx, Slide 34; tracing from Slide 35
set1.alt: Twelve-lead electrocardiogram on grid paper, with each lead labeled

set1.io: Recognize common pacemaker rhythms and pacing artifacts.
set1.q: A 78-year-old man has the 12-lead shown. What are the sharp, narrow vertical lines just before each wide QRS?
opts: Delta waves
Delta waves are slurred, gradual upstrokes of the QRS in preexcitation; these are instantaneous vertical spikes.
P waves
P waves are rounded atrial deflections; these are sharp, narrow lines that precede each paced QRS.
Pacing spikes
Correct. Each sharp vertical line is the pacemaker's spike, the pacing artifact, followed by the wide QRS it produces in a ventricular paced rhythm.
Osborn waves
Osborn waves are notches at the end of the QRS, in hypothermia and early repolarization; these lines come before it.
set1.cite: 16. EKG Pericarditis Electrolytes and Other Abnormalities.pptx, Slide 14
set1.alt: Twelve-lead electrocardiogram on grid paper, with each lead labeled

set1.io: Compare and contrast ECG manifestations of electrolyte abnormalities.
set1.q: A 52-year-old man has the leads shown, with flattened T waves and the arrowed waves after them. Which electrolyte disturbance best explains this?
opts: Hypokalemia
Correct. Hypokalemia (serum potassium below 3.5 mEq/L) prolongs repolarization: T-wave flattening, prominent U waves and ST depression are its classic signs.
Hyperkalemia
Hyperkalemia peaks the T wave; flattened T waves with prominent U waves are its opposite.
Hypercalcemia
Hypercalcemia shortens the ST segment and QTc so the T wave hugs the QRS; it does not bring out U waves.
Hypocalcemia
Hypocalcemia lengthens the ST segment but leaves the T wave normally shaped, without prominent U waves.
set1.cite: 16. EKG Pericarditis Electrolytes and Other Abnormalities.pptx, Slide 37; tracing from Slide 38
set1.alt: Leads V4, V5 and V6 on grid paper, with red arrows pointing to part of each beat

set1.io: Topic — Preexcitation and accessory pathway tachycardias
set1.q: A 30-year-old man with a known accessory pathway has a regular, wide, monomorphic tachycardia, shown here. Which rhythm is most likely?
opts: Orthodromic reentrant tachycardia
Orthodromic reentry goes down the normal pathway, so its tachycardia is narrow.
Sinus tachycardia
Sinus tachycardia has normal P waves before narrow QRS complexes; this is a wide-complex tachycardia.
Antidromic reentrant tachycardia
Correct. Antidromic atrioventricular reentrant tachycardia conducts down the accessory pathway and back up the normal pathway, producing a regular, monomorphic, wide tachycardia.
Ventricular paced rhythm
A paced rhythm shows a spike before each QRS at a programmed rate, not a wide tachycardia like this.
set1.cite: 16. EKG Pericarditis Electrolytes and Other Abnormalities.pptx, Slide 33
set1.alt: Three-lead rhythm strip on grid paper at a fast rate

set1.io: Topic — Thyroid disorders
set1.q: A 36-year-old woman has hyperthyroidism. Which tracing finding is the most commonly observed?
opts: Atrial fibrillation
Atrial fibrillation is the second most common finding in hyperthyroidism, after sinus tachycardia.
Sinus bradycardia
Sinus bradycardia is the hypothyroid finding, from a slowed metabolic rate.
Global low voltage
Global low-voltage QRS complexes belong to hypothyroidism, not to an adrenergic, hyperthyroid state.
Sinus tachycardia
Correct. Hyperthyroidism is a state of adrenergic hyperactivity, so sinus tachycardia is the most commonly observed finding; atrial fibrillation is the second most common.
set1.cite: 16. EKG Pericarditis Electrolytes and Other Abnormalities.pptx, Slide 44

set1.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with: Benign Early Repolarization (BER), acute pericarditis, long QT syndrome
set1.q: A 34-year-old man has had chest pain for two days. His 12-lead is shown. Which diagnosis best fits the tracing?
opts: Inferior ST-elevation infarction
An inferior infarction elevates II, III and aVF with reciprocal depression in I and aVL; this elevation is global and concave with no reciprocal changes.
Benign early repolarization
Early repolarization also shows global concave elevation, but not the PR-segment depression seen here; it carries J-point notching instead.
Acute pericarditis
Correct. Global concave ST elevation with PR-segment depression, PR elevation in aVR and no reciprocal ST depression outside aVR and V1 is acute pericarditis.
Brugada syndrome
Brugada changes are isolated to V1 to V3 (coved or saddleback elevation); this tracing's elevation is global.
set1.cite: 16. EKG Pericarditis Electrolytes and Other Abnormalities.pptx, Slide 6
set1.alt: Twelve-lead electrocardiogram on grid paper, with each lead labeled

set1.io: Topic — Preexcitation and accessory pathway tachycardias
set1.q: A 20-year-old woman's 12-lead is shown. What is the slurred upstroke at the start of each QRS called?
opts: A J wave
A J (Osborn) wave is a notch at the end of the QRS, in hypothermia and early repolarization.
A U wave
A U wave follows the T wave and is prominent in hypokalemia.
A pacing spike
A pacing spike is a sharp vertical artifact before a paced QRS, not a gradual slur.
A delta wave
Correct. The delta wave is a slurring of the QRS upstroke: impulses bypass the atrioventricular node through the accessory pathway and begin depolarizing the ventricles early.
set1.cite: 16. EKG Pericarditis Electrolytes and Other Abnormalities.pptx, Slide 27; tracing from Slide 29
set1.alt: Twelve-lead electrocardiogram on grid paper, with each lead labeled

set1.io: Compare and contrast ECG findings associated with: BER, acute pericarditis, STEMI patterns
set1.q: A 71-year-old man with a ventricular paced rhythm has chest pain. Which finding meets Sgarbossa's criteria?
opts: Discordant elevation of 2 mm
Discordant elevation counts only at 5 mm or more, in a lead with a negative QRS.
Concordant elevation, 1 mm or more
Correct. Concordant ST elevation of 1 mm or more in any lead with a positive QRS complex meets Sgarbossa's criteria for acute infarction in a paced rhythm or left bundle branch block.
A wide QRS complex
A wide QRS is expected in a paced rhythm; it is the background, not a criterion.
T waves opposite the QRS
T waves pointing opposite the QRS (discordant, contralateral) are normal for paced rhythms and left bundle branch block.
set1.cite: 16. EKG Pericarditis Electrolytes and Other Abnormalities.pptx, Slide 18

set1.io: Compare and contrast ECG findings associated with: BER, acute pericarditis, STEMI patterns
set1.q: A 30-year-old man of Southeast Asian descent fainted at rest. His 12-lead is shown. Which diagnosis fits the pattern in V1 and V2?
opts: Type 1 Brugada pattern
Correct. Coved (convex) ST elevation isolated to V1 to V3 in a young man of Southeast Asian descent is the type 1, coved-shaped Brugada pattern.
Type 2 Brugada pattern
Type 2 is the saddleback shape, with the ST segment dipping before the T wave; these right precordial leads are coved.
Anteroseptal infarction
An anteroseptal infarction elevates V1 to V4 in a patient with ischemic symptoms; the coved shape confined to V1 to V3 in a young man is Brugada.
Benign early repolarization
Early repolarization is global and concave with J-point notching, not coved elevation confined to the right precordial leads.
set1.cite: 16. EKG Pericarditis Electrolytes and Other Abnormalities.pptx, Slide 11
set1.alt: Twelve-lead electrocardiogram on grid paper, with each lead labeled

set1.io: Recognize ECG changes associated with: digoxin toxicity, amiodarone toxicity, tricyclic antidepressant toxicity
set1.q: A 21-year-old woman took an overdose of a tricyclic antidepressant. Which pair of tracing changes does the overdose produce?
opts: QT prolongation and tachycardia
Correct. A tricyclic overdose prolongs the QT and, through anticholinergic activity, speeds the heart; its fast sodium-channel blockade also widens the QRS.
QT shortening and bradycardia
Both go the wrong way: a tricyclic overdose prolongs the QT and speeds the heart through anticholinergic activity.
Peaked T waves and flat P waves
Peaked T waves with flattened P waves are the hyperkalemia progression, not a tricyclic overdose.
Delta waves and a short PR
A delta wave with a short PR interval is preexcitation through an accessory pathway, not a drug effect.
set1.cite: 16. EKG Pericarditis Electrolytes and Other Abnormalities.pptx, Slide 49

set1.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with: COPD/COLD, pulmonary embolism, hypothermia
set1.q: A 75-year-old man was found outdoors on a winter night. His 12-lead is shown. What are the notches at the end of each QRS?
opts: Delta waves
Delta waves are slurred upstrokes at the start of the QRS in preexcitation; these notches sit at its end.
Osborn waves
Correct. Below 32°C (90°F), Osborn (J) waves appear as notches at the end of the QRS, and they are frequently mistaken for an ST-elevation infarction.
Prominent U waves
U waves follow the T wave and are a hypokalemia sign; these notches are at the junction of the QRS and ST segment.
Pacing artifacts
Pacing artifacts are sharp spikes BEFORE a paced QRS, not rounded notches after it.
set1.cite: 16. EKG Pericarditis Electrolytes and Other Abnormalities.pptx, Slide 16; tracing from Slide 17
set1.alt: Twelve-lead electrocardiogram on grid paper, with each lead labeled

set1.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with: Benign Early Repolarization (BER), acute pericarditis, long QT syndrome
set1.q: A 24-year-old man's 12-lead is shown: concave ST elevation with notched J points and no reciprocal depression. What clinical significance does this pattern carry?
opts: It signals an evolving infarction
An infarction shows localized elevation with reciprocal depression; diffuse concave elevation with J waves and no reciprocal change is the benign variant.
None; it is a normal variant
Correct. Benign early repolarization, also called normal variant ST elevation, is seen mostly in young men and has no clinical significance.
It predicts sudden cardiac death
Arrhythmia risk belongs to Brugada syndrome, an inherited arrhythmogenic disease with V1 to V3 changes, not to benign early repolarization.
It indicates pericardial inflammation
Pericardial inflammation adds PR-segment depression; benign early repolarization has no clinical significance.
set1.cite: 16. EKG Pericarditis Electrolytes and Other Abnormalities.pptx, Slide 7; tracing from Slide 8
set1.alt: Twelve-lead electrocardiogram on grid paper, with each lead labeled

set1.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with: COPD/COLD, pulmonary embolism, hypothermia
set1.q: A 78-year-old woman's core temperature is falling toward 35°C (95°F; normal is about 37°C). Which tracing change occurs first?
opts: Osborn waves
Osborn waves become apparent only below 32°C (90°F), after bradycardia and interval prolongation.
Sinus tachycardia
Cooling slows the sinus rate; sinus tachycardia is the commonest finding of hyperthyroidism.
Peaked T waves
Peaked T waves are the early sign of hyperkalemia, not of cooling.
Sinus bradycardia
Correct. As the body temperature approaches 35°C (95°F) sinus bradycardia occurs; the intervals then prolong, and below 32°C (90°F) Osborn waves appear.
set1.cite: 16. EKG Pericarditis Electrolytes and Other Abnormalities.pptx, Slide 16

set1.io: Topic — Preexcitation and accessory pathway tachycardias
set1.q: A 27-year-old woman with an accessory pathway has the narrow-complex tachycardia shown. Which route does the circuit take?
opts: Down the accessory, up the normal pathway
That is the antidromic circuit, which depolarizes the ventricles through the accessory pathway and produces a wide tachycardia.
Down the normal pathway, up the accessory
Correct. In orthodromic reentry, conduction toward the ventricles (anterograde) goes through the normal pathway and returns up the accessory pathway, so the QRS stays narrow.
Around the right ventricular outflow tract
The right ventricular outflow tract is the site of Brugada syndrome's sodium-channel disease, not a reentry circuit.
Through the sinoatrial node alone
Reentry needs a circuit: here the normal pathway and the accessory pathway together.
set1.cite: 16. EKG Pericarditis Electrolytes and Other Abnormalities.pptx, Slide 30; tracing from Slide 32
set1.alt: Twelve-lead electrocardiogram on grid paper, with each lead labeled

set1.io: Compare and contrast ECG findings associated with: BER, acute pericarditis, STEMI patterns
set1.q: A 26-year-old man's lead V6 shows much more T wave than ST elevation. Which diagnosis does this favor?
opts: Acute pericarditis
Pericarditis has more ST elevation relative to the T wave, an ST-to-T ratio above 25% in V6.
Hypercalcemia
Hypercalcemia shortens the ST segment until the T wave sits on the QRS; it is not judged by the V6 ratio.
Type 2 Brugada
Brugada changes are confined to V1 to V3 and are not judged by the V6 ratio.
Early repolarization
Correct. In early repolarization there is more T wave than ST elevation in V6 (ratio under 25%); pericarditis has more ST elevation than T wave.
set1.cite: 16. EKG Pericarditis Electrolytes and Other Abnormalities.pptx, Slide 9

set1.io: Compare and contrast ECG manifestations of electrolyte abnormalities.
set1.q: A 57-year-old woman's serum calcium is low, 7.4 mg/dL (reference range 8.5 to 10.5). Why does her ST segment lengthen?
opts: Phase 2 of the action potential is shortened
Shortening phase 2 is hypercalcemia, which shortens the ST segment.
Phase 2 of the action potential is prolonged
Correct. Hypocalcemia prolongs the duration of phase 2 of the cardiac action potential, which prolongs the ST segment without changing the T wave, and so prolongs the QTc.
Phase 0 of the action potential is delayed
Phase 0 is the sodium upstroke, slowed by sodium-channel blockers; calcium acts on phase 2.
Repolarization of the atria is delayed
The ST segment reflects the ventricular plateau, phase 2, which low calcium prolongs.
set1.cite: 16. EKG Pericarditis Electrolytes and Other Abnormalities.pptx, Slide 40

set1.io: Topic — Preexcitation and accessory pathway tachycardias
set1.q: A 26-year-old man with an accessory pathway develops a sustained reentrant tachycardia. What typically starts it?
opts: A premature beat near the pathway
Correct. A premature atrial or ventricular complex occurring near the accessory pathway can initiate premature depolarization, and the pathway plus the normal pathway form a reentry circuit.
Sudden cooling below 32 degrees Celsius
Cooling below 32 degrees Celsius produces Osborn waves; it is not the trigger of accessory pathway reentry.
A rise in serum calcium
High calcium shortens the ST segment; it is not what starts accessory pathway reentry.
Inflammation of the pericardium
Pericarditis produces global concave ST elevation, not reentrant tachycardia.
set1.cite: 16. EKG Pericarditis Electrolytes and Other Abnormalities.pptx, Slide 30

set1.io: Topic — Thyroid disorders
set1.q: A 67-year-old woman has hypothyroidism. Which tracing finding fits her condition?
opts: Sinus tachycardia
Sinus tachycardia is the commonest hyperthyroid finding, from adrenergic hyperactivity.
A shortened QTc
Hypothyroidism prolongs the QTc; a short QTc is hypercalcemia.
Peaked T waves
Peaked T waves are hyperkalemia; hypothyroid T waves are flattened or inverted.
Low-voltage QRS
Correct. Hypothyroidism slows metabolism and contractility: sinus bradycardia with global low-voltage QRS complexes, flattened or inverted T waves, a prolonged QTc and low-amplitude P waves.
set1.cite: 16. EKG Pericarditis Electrolytes and Other Abnormalities.pptx, Slide 44

set1.io: Compare and contrast ECG findings associated with: BER, acute pericarditis, STEMI patterns
set1.q: A 31-year-old woman has global concave ST elevation. Her lead V6 is shown, with the ST elevation boxed in blue and the T-wave height in red. Which diagnosis does the ratio favor?
opts: Benign early repolarization
Early repolarization gives a V6 ST/T ratio under 25%, with much more T wave than ST elevation; this ratio is higher.
Acute pericarditis
Correct. The ST elevation is about half the T-wave height. An ST/T ratio above 25% in V6 suggests pericarditis: more ST elevation than T wave (the V6 phenomenon).
Brugada syndrome
Brugada changes are isolated to V1 to V3; the V6 ratio separates pericarditis from early repolarization.
Hypercalcemia
Hypercalcemia shortens the ST segment until the T wave sits against the QRS; it does not raise the ST/T ratio.
set1.cite: 16. EKG Pericarditis Electrolytes and Other Abnormalities.pptx, Slide 9
set1.alt: Lead V6 rhythm strip with a blue box and a red box drawn over one beat

set1.io: Recognize ECG changes associated with: digoxin toxicity, amiodarone toxicity, tricyclic antidepressant toxicity
set1.q: A 72-year-old man has amiodarone toxicity. Which actions produce its tracing changes?
opts: Sodium-potassium pump inhibition
Pump inhibition is digoxin's mechanism; amiodarone blocks the ion channels themselves.
Anticholinergic activity alone
Anticholinergic activity is a tricyclic antidepressant effect, causing tachycardia.
Multi-channel and beta blockade
Correct. Amiodarone blocks sodium, potassium and calcium channels and also acts as a beta blocker in the heart, reducing conduction velocity.
An accessory conduction pathway
An accessory pathway is an anatomic bypass (Wolff-Parkinson-White), not a drug action.
set1.cite: 16. EKG Pericarditis Electrolytes and Other Abnormalities.pptx, Slide 48

set1.topic: Left bundle branch block and pacing
set1.io: Compare and contrast ECG findings associated with: BER, acute pericarditis, STEMI patterns
set1.q: A 70-year-old man with chest pain has a left bundle branch block, shown here. Why is an ST-elevation infarction hard to locate on this tracing?
opts: The block hides all ST segments
The ST segments are still visible; the problem is that the block itself distorts them globally.
Wide QRS with global ST and T changes
Correct. Left bundle branch blocks and ventricular paced rhythms cause wide QRS complexes with global ST elevation and T-wave changes, which make an ST-elevation infarction difficult to locate.
Bundle branch blocks prevent infarction
A block does not protect the heart; it only makes an infarction harder to see.
The heart rate is always too fast
The difficulty is the widened, distorted ventricular complex, not the rate.
set1.cite: 16. EKG Pericarditis Electrolytes and Other Abnormalities.pptx, Slide 13; tracing from Slide 15
set1.alt: Twelve-lead electrocardiogram on grid paper, with each lead labeled

set1.io: Compare and contrast ECG findings associated with: BER, acute pericarditis, STEMI patterns
set1.q: A 28-year-old man's 12-lead is shown, with ST elevation in V2. Which pattern is this?
opts: Type 2 Brugada (saddleback)
Correct. Saddle-shaped (saddleback) ST elevation in V1 to V3 is type 2 Brugada; type 1 is the coved, convex shape.
Type 1 Brugada (coved)
Type 1 is coved, convex elevation sloping straight down into the T wave; the saddle shape is type 2.
Acute pericarditis
Pericarditis elevates the ST segment globally with PR depression, not in a saddle shape confined to V1 to V3.
Hyperkalemia
Hyperkalemia shows peaked, symmetric T waves, then flattened P waves and a wide QRS; it has no saddle-shaped ST segment.
set1.cite: 16. EKG Pericarditis Electrolytes and Other Abnormalities.pptx, Slide 12
set1.alt: Twelve-lead electrocardiogram on grid paper, with each lead labeled

set1.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with: Benign Early Repolarization (BER), acute pericarditis, long QT syndrome
set1.q: A healthy 25-year-old man's lead V4 is shown. What is the circled notch at the end of the QRS called?
opts: A J wave
Correct. Terminal QRS notching in benign early repolarization is known as the J wave (also the fishhook sign, or Osborn wave).
A delta wave
A delta wave is a slur at the start of the QRS from preexcitation; this notch sits at the end.
A U wave
A U wave follows the T wave and is prominent in hypokalemia; this notch is at the junction of the QRS and ST segment.
A pathologic Q wave
A Q wave is the first negative deflection of the QRS; this is a positive notch at its end.
set1.cite: 16. EKG Pericarditis Electrolytes and Other Abnormalities.pptx, Slide 7
set1.alt: Lead V4 rhythm strip with one area circled in red

set1.io: Recognize ECG changes associated with: hyperkalemia, hypokalemia, hypercalcemia, hypocalcemia
set1.q: A 63-year-old woman on dialysis missed three sessions. Her 12-lead is shown, with very wide QRS complexes and no visible P waves. Which disturbance best explains it?
opts: Hypokalemia
Hypokalemia flattens T waves and brings out U waves; it does not erase the P waves and widen the QRS like this.
Hypercalcemia
Hypercalcemia shortens the ST segment and QTc; it does not widen the QRS or remove the P waves.
Severe hyperkalemia
Correct. As potassium climbs, the P waves flatten away and the QRS widens toward a sine wave: late, severe hyperkalemia.
Hypothyroidism
Hypothyroidism gives low-voltage complexes with sinus bradycardia, not this very wide QRS.
set1.cite: 16. EKG Pericarditis Electrolytes and Other Abnormalities.pptx, Slide 36
set1.alt: Twelve-lead electrocardiogram on grid paper, with each lead labeled

set2.io: Compare and contrast ECG findings associated with: BER, acute pericarditis, STEMI patterns
set2.q: A 62-year-old woman with a left bundle branch block has chest pain; her 12-lead is shown. How much discordant ST elevation meets Sgarbossa's criteria?
opts: 1 mm or more
One millimeter is the threshold for concordant elevation; discordant elevation must reach 5 mm or more.
2 mm or more
Two millimeters of discordant elevation is within what a left bundle branch block can produce; the criterion is 5 mm or more.
Any amount at all
Some discordant elevation is normal for a left bundle branch block, so a threshold of 5 mm or more is used.
5 mm or more
Correct. Discordant ST elevation of 5 mm or more in any lead with a negative QRS complex is a Sgarbossa criterion; smaller discordant elevation can be expected in the block.
set2.cite: 16. EKG Pericarditis Electrolytes and Other Abnormalities.pptx, Slide 18; tracing from Slide 19
set2.alt: Twelve-lead electrocardiogram on grid paper, with each lead labeled

set2.io: Topic — Preexcitation and accessory pathway tachycardias
set2.q: A 35-year-old woman has the wide regular tachycardia shown and does not know whether she has an accessory pathway. How is the correct interpretation made?
opts: Find delta waves in sinus rhythm

Correct. The tracing alone may not separate antidromic reentry from ventricular tachycardia, which it is treated as until proven otherwise; once cardioversion restores sinus rhythm, a delta wave on that tracing reveals the pathway.
Measure the V6 ST-to-T ratio
The V6 ratio separates pericarditis from early repolarization; it cannot tell antidromic reentry from ventricular tachycardia.
Apply Sgarbossa's criteria
Sgarbossa's criteria find an infarction in a left bundle branch block or paced rhythm, not an accessory pathway.
Read the rate from the strip
The rate alone cannot separate the two; at times the difference cannot be told from the tracing at all.
set2.cite: 16. EKG Pericarditis Electrolytes and Other Abnormalities.pptx, Slide 31; tracing from Slide 33
set2.alt: Three-lead rhythm strip on grid paper at a fast rate

set2.io: Recognize ECG changes associated with: digoxin toxicity, amiodarone toxicity, tricyclic antidepressant toxicity
set2.q: A 69-year-old woman on amiodarone has a prolonged QT. Which effect of the drug explains it?
opts: It slows phase 3
Correct. Amiodarone slows phase 3 of the cardiac action potential, causing QT prolongation; it also suppresses sinoatrial automaticity and slows atrioventricular conduction.
It shortens phase 2
Shortening phase 2 would shorten the ST segment and QT, as hypercalcemia does.
It speeds phase 0
Amiodarone reduces conduction velocity; it does not speed the sodium upstroke.
It adds a delta wave
A delta wave comes from an accessory pathway, not from a drug.
set2.cite: 16. EKG Pericarditis Electrolytes and Other Abnormalities.pptx, Slide 48

set2.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with: COPD/COLD, pulmonary embolism, hypothermia
set2.q: A 50-year-old woman has sudden severe shortness of breath with clear, equal lung sounds. Her 12-lead is shown. Which pattern on it is associated with pulmonary embolism?
opts: Coved elevation in V1 to V3
Coved elevation confined to V1 to V3 is type 1 Brugada, not pulmonary embolism.
A delta wave
A delta wave marks preexcitation through an accessory pathway.
S1Q3T3
Correct. A deep S wave in lead I, a Q wave in lead III and an inverted T wave in lead III, the S1Q3T3 pattern, is the classic pulmonary embolism finding, with sinus tachycardia.
Peaked T waves
Peaked, symmetric T waves are the early sign of hyperkalemia.
set2.cite: 16. EKG Pericarditis Electrolytes and Other Abnormalities.pptx, Slide 50
set2.alt: Twelve-lead electrocardiogram on grid paper, with each lead labeled

set2.io: Compare and contrast ECG manifestations of electrolyte abnormalities.
set2.q: A 64-year-old man has a serum sodium of 129 mEq/L (reference range 135 to 145). What change does this sodium level make to his tracing?
opts: Peaked T waves
Peaked T waves are the early sign of hyperkalemia, a potassium disturbance; sodium changes leave the tracing alone.
No change at all
Correct. Alterations in sodium levels do not cause any tracing or rhythm changes; it is potassium and calcium disturbances that change the tracing.
A prolonged QTc
A prolonged QTc with a long ST segment is a hypocalcemia finding; sodium changes do not alter the tracing.
Prominent U waves
Prominent U waves are a hypokalemia sign; altered sodium levels cause no tracing or rhythm change.
set2.cite: 16. EKG Pericarditis Electrolytes and Other Abnormalities.pptx, Slide 46

set2.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with: Benign Early Repolarization (BER), acute pericarditis, long QT syndrome
set2.q: A 33-year-old man is diagnosed with pericarditis. Which space is inflamed?
opts: Between endocardium and myocardium
Pericarditis involves the pericardium, outside the heart muscle; the endocardium lines the chambers inside.
Within the right ventricular outflow tract
The right ventricular outflow tract's sodium channels are affected in Brugada syndrome, not pericarditis.
Between visceral and parietal pericardium
Correct. Pericarditis refers to inflammation of the space between the visceral and parietal pericardium, which also involves the atria, hence the PR changes.
Within the coronary artery wall
Plaque within the coronary artery wall causes ischemic heart disease; pericarditis inflames the pericardium.
set2.cite: 16. EKG Pericarditis Electrolytes and Other Abnormalities.pptx, Slide 5

set2.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with: Benign Early Repolarization (BER), acute pericarditis, long QT syndrome
set2.q: A 29-year-old woman has the 12-lead shown, with global concave ST elevation. Which finding in lead aVR supports pericarditis?
opts: ST-segment elevation
aVR is one of the two leads where pericarditis may show ST depression; elevation in aVR is not its sign.
PR-segment elevation
Correct. Pericarditis inflames the atria too, so the PR segment is depressed in most leads and elevated in aVR, alongside global concave ST elevation.
A pathologic Q wave
Q waves anywhere on the tracing argue against pericarditis and mean an acute infarction must be considered.
A delta wave
A delta wave is the slurred QRS upstroke of preexcitation; it has nothing to do with pericardial inflammation.
set2.cite: 16. EKG Pericarditis Electrolytes and Other Abnormalities.pptx, Slide 6
set2.alt: Twelve-lead electrocardiogram on grid paper, with each lead labeled

set2.io: Recognize ECG changes associated with: hyperkalemia, hypokalemia, hypercalcemia, hypocalcemia
set2.q: A 45-year-old woman's leads V4 to V6 are shown. What are the arrowed waves that follow each T wave?
opts: Delta waves
A delta wave slurs the start of the QRS in preexcitation; these waves come after the T wave.
Osborn waves
Osborn waves are notches at the end of the QRS in hypothermia, not waves after the T wave.
Second P waves
These waves follow the T wave closely in every beat; prominent waves in that position are U waves.
U waves
Correct. A small wave after the T wave is a U wave. Prominent U waves, with T-wave flattening, are classic signs of hypokalemia, which prolongs repolarization.
set2.cite: 16. EKG Pericarditis Electrolytes and Other Abnormalities.pptx, Slide 38
set2.alt: Leads V4, V5 and V6 on grid paper, with red arrows pointing to part of each beat

set2.io: Compare and contrast ECG findings associated with: BER, acute pericarditis, STEMI patterns
set2.q: A 31-year-old man's V1 to V3 show convex, coved ST elevation. Which Brugada type is this?
opts: Type 1
Correct. Type 1 Brugada is convex ST elevation in V1 to V3, also called the coved-shaped type.
Type 2
Type 2 Brugada is the saddle-shaped ST elevation (carousel horses sign), not coved.
Type A
Types A and B are Wolff-Parkinson-White pathways (left or right Kent bundle), not Brugada patterns.
Type B
Type B is a right-sided Kent bundle in Wolff-Parkinson-White, with a mostly negative QRS in V1.
set2.cite: 16. EKG Pericarditis Electrolytes and Other Abnormalities.pptx, Slide 10

set2.io: Recognize common pacemaker rhythms and pacing artifacts.
set2.q: An 81-year-old woman has the 12-lead shown. Which rhythm is it?
opts: Left bundle branch block
A left bundle branch block also gives wide QRS complexes and global ST and T changes, but there is no pacing spike before each complex.
Ventricular paced rhythm
Correct. A sharp pacing spike before each wide QRS, with T waves pointing opposite the QRS (contralateral T waves) and global ST changes, is a ventricular paced rhythm.
Ventricular tachycardia
Ventricular tachycardia is a fast wide-complex rhythm without pacing spikes; this rate is not fast and every beat is preceded by a spike.
Wolff-Parkinson-White pattern
Wolff-Parkinson-White shows a short PR interval and a slurred delta wave, not a pacing spike before each QRS.
set2.cite: 16. EKG Pericarditis Electrolytes and Other Abnormalities.pptx, Slide 14
set2.alt: Twelve-lead electrocardiogram on grid paper, with each lead labeled

set2.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with: COPD/COLD, pulmonary embolism, hypothermia
set2.q: A 58-year-old man has a large pulmonary embolism. Which axis change does his tracing tend to show?
opts: A leftward axis shift
The strained, dilated chamber is the right ventricle, which pulls the axis rightward.
No axis change is possible
Right ventricular dilation does shift the axis, toward the right.
A rightward axis shift
Correct. Dilation and enlargement of the right ventricle under high pressure causes more of a rightward axis deviation in pulmonary embolism.
An axis that alternates beats
Alternating beats suggest bigeminy (as in digoxin toxicity), not a pulmonary embolism axis change.
set2.cite: 16. EKG Pericarditis Electrolytes and Other Abnormalities.pptx, Slide 50

set2.io: Topic — Preexcitation and accessory pathway tachycardias
set2.q: A 23-year-old man with a known accessory pathway has sudden palpitations. His regular, narrow-complex tachycardia is shown. Which rhythm is this?
opts: Antidromic reentrant tachycardia
Antidromic conduction runs down the accessory pathway first, so the ventricles depolarize abnormally and the tachycardia is wide.
Ventricular tachycardia
Ventricular tachycardia is a wide-complex tachycardia; these complexes are narrow.
Orthodromic reentrant tachycardia
Correct. Orthodromic atrioventricular reentrant tachycardia conducts down the normal pathway and back up the accessory pathway, producing a regular narrow-complex tachycardia.
Ventricular paced rhythm
A paced rhythm has a spike before each wide QRS and a set rate, not a narrow-complex tachycardia.
set2.cite: 16. EKG Pericarditis Electrolytes and Other Abnormalities.pptx, Slide 32
set2.alt: Twelve-lead electrocardiogram on grid paper, with each lead labeled

set2.io: Recognize ECG changes associated with: hyperkalemia, hypokalemia, hypercalcemia, hypocalcemia
set2.q: A 48-year-old woman has the 12-lead shown: a long, flat ST segment before a normally shaped T wave. Which electrolyte disturbance does it suggest?
opts: Hypocalcemia
Correct. Hypocalcemia prolongs phase 2 of the action potential, so the ST segment lengthens while the T wave keeps a normal shape and duration, and the QTc is prolonged.
Hypercalcemia
Hypercalcemia shortens the ST segment until the T wave sits against the QRS.
Hyperkalemia
Hyperkalemia peaks the T wave rather than lengthening the ST segment before a normal one.
Hypokalemia
Hypokalemia flattens the T wave and adds prominent U waves; the T wave here is normal.
set2.cite: 16. EKG Pericarditis Electrolytes and Other Abnormalities.pptx, Slide 41
set2.alt: Twelve-lead electrocardiogram on grid paper, with each lead labeled

set2.io: Recognize ECG changes associated with: hyperkalemia, hypokalemia, hypercalcemia, hypocalcemia
set2.q: A 68-year-old woman has hyperkalemia. Besides its classic signs, which other changes can it produce?
opts: Blocks and ST elevation
Correct. Hyperkalemia can cause a host of changes, such as bradycardias, tachycardias, ST elevation, T-wave abnormalities and atrioventricular and bundle branch blocks.
Delta waves and a short PR
Delta waves with a short PR come from an accessory pathway, not from potassium.
Osborn waves only
Osborn waves are the terminal notches of hypothermia and early repolarization.
No other changes at all
Hyperkalemia is notable for producing many different changes beyond its classic signs.
set2.cite: 16. EKG Pericarditis Electrolytes and Other Abnormalities.pptx, Slide 34

set2.io: Compare and contrast ECG findings associated with: BER, acute pericarditis, STEMI patterns
set2.q: A 30-year-old woman's tracing could be pericarditis or benign early repolarization. Which lead is used to tell them apart?
opts: aVR
aVR is where pericarditis shows PR ELEVATION; the ST-to-T ratio is measured in V6.
V6
Correct. Lead V6 is used: the ST elevation height is compared with the T-wave amplitude in V6, called the lead V6 phenomenon.
V1
V1 is one of the two leads where reciprocal depression is allowed in both; the ratio is taken in V6.
III
Lead III is an inferior lead; the comparison of ST height with T amplitude uses V6.
set2.cite: 16. EKG Pericarditis Electrolytes and Other Abnormalities.pptx, Slide 9

set2.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with: COPD/COLD, pulmonary embolism, hypothermia
set2.q: A 70-year-old man with hypothermia has prominent Osborn waves. Which diagnosis are they frequently mistaken for?
opts: Wolff-Parkinson-White
Wolff-Parkinson-White has a delta wave at the start of the QRS; Osborn waves sit at its end and mimic ST elevation.
ST-elevation infarction
Correct. Below 32°C (90°F) Osborn waves become apparent and are frequently mistaken for an ST-elevation infarction.
Hypokalemia
Hypokalemia's prominent U waves come after the T wave; Osborn waves are terminal QRS notches that look like ST elevation.
Hypothyroidism
Hypothyroidism gives low voltage and bradycardia; Osborn waves are mistaken for infarction.
set2.cite: 16. EKG Pericarditis Electrolytes and Other Abnormalities.pptx, Slide 16

set2.io: Topic — Preexcitation and accessory pathway tachycardias
set2.q: A 32-year-old man has antidromic reentrant tachycardia. Which rhythm can it be impossible to tell apart from on the tracing alone?
opts: Sinus bradycardia
Antidromic reentry is a fast, wide tachycardia, nothing like sinus bradycardia.
Ventricular tachycardia

Correct. At times it is impossible to tell antidromic reentry from ventricular tachycardia (and orthodromic reentry from supraventricular tachycardia) by the tracing alone; history helps if the patient knows of a pathway.
Benign early repolarization
Early repolarization is a resting ST pattern in young men, not a tachycardia.
Hypothermia
Hypothermia slows the heart and produces Osborn waves; it is not a wide tachycardia.
set2.cite: 16. EKG Pericarditis Electrolytes and Other Abnormalities.pptx, Slide 31

set2.io: Compare and contrast ECG manifestations of electrolyte abnormalities.
set2.q: A 60-year-old man with a high serum calcium has the 12-lead shown. Which phase of the cardiac action potential is shortened to produce it?
opts: Phase 0
Phase 0 is the rapid sodium upstroke; calcium disorders act on the phase 2 plateau.
Phase 3
Phase 3 is the repolarization slowed by amiodarone's potassium-channel block, which prolongs the QT; calcium acts on phase 2.
Phase 2
Correct. Hypercalcemia shortens phase 2 (the plateau), which shortens the ST segment and the QTc; hypocalcemia prolongs the same phase.
Phase 4
Phase 4 is the resting phase between beats; the ST segment reflects phase 2.
set2.cite: 16. EKG Pericarditis Electrolytes and Other Abnormalities.pptx, Slide 42; tracing from Slide 43
set2.alt: Twelve-lead electrocardiogram on grid paper, with each lead labeled

set2.io: Recognize ECG changes associated with: digoxin toxicity, amiodarone toxicity, tricyclic antidepressant toxicity
set2.q: An 84-year-old man on digoxin has the rhythm strip shown. Which abnormality is the most common one in digoxin toxicity?
opts: Frequent premature ventricular beats
Correct. Digoxin toxicity inhibits the sodium-potassium pump and makes cells abnormally excitable; frequent premature ventricular complexes are its most common abnormality.
A delta wave with a short PR
A delta wave with a short PR is Wolff-Parkinson-White preexcitation, not digoxin toxicity.
Coved ST elevation in V1 to V3
Coved V1 to V3 elevation is type 1 Brugada, an inherited sodium-channel disease.
Osborn waves
Osborn waves are terminal QRS notches of hypothermia and early repolarization.
set2.cite: 16. EKG Pericarditis Electrolytes and Other Abnormalities.pptx, Slide 47
set2.alt: A single-lead rhythm strip on grid paper

set2.io: Recognize ECG changes associated with: digoxin toxicity, amiodarone toxicity, tricyclic antidepressant toxicity
set2.q: A 19-year-old man has the 12-lead shown after a tricyclic antidepressant overdose. Which interval change fits the overdose?
opts: A shortened QTc
A shortened QTc is the hypercalcemia pattern; tricyclic overdose prolongs the QT.
A short PR interval
A short PR interval with a delta wave is preexcitation through an accessory pathway.
A shortened ST segment
A shortened ST segment is the hypercalcemia finding, from a shortened phase 2.
QT prolongation
Correct. A tricyclic overdose prolongs the QT; its fast sodium-channel blockade also widens the QRS, as on this tracing, and its anticholinergic activity adds tachycardia.
set2.cite: 16. EKG Pericarditis Electrolytes and Other Abnormalities.pptx, Slide 49
set2.alt: Twelve-lead electrocardiogram on grid paper, with each lead labeled

set2.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with: Benign Early Repolarization (BER), acute pericarditis, long QT syndrome
set2.q: A 23-year-old man's report reads benign early repolarization. Which other name does this pattern carry?
opts: Coved-type ST elevation
Coved-type elevation is type 1 Brugada, an inherited arrhythmogenic disease, not a benign variant.
Transmural injury
Transmural injury is ST elevation from full-thickness ischemia, an infarction in progress.
Normal variant ST elevation
Correct. Benign early repolarization is also known as normal variant ST elevation: a benign pattern with no clinical significance.
The lead V6 phenomenon
The lead V6 phenomenon is the ST-to-T ratio test that separates pericarditis from early repolarization, not a name for the pattern.
set2.cite: 16. EKG Pericarditis Electrolytes and Other Abnormalities.pptx, Slide 7

set2.io: Topic — Preexcitation and accessory pathway tachycardias
set2.q: A 24-year-old woman's tracing shows a delta wave. What causes the slurring?
opts: Delayed atrial repolarization
Atrial repolarization is not what slurs the QRS upstroke; early ventricular activation through the accessory pathway does.
A pacemaker spike
A pacing spike is a sharp artifact, not a gradual slur of the QRS.
Early depolarization via the bypass

Correct. The slurring occurs as impulses bypass the atrioventricular node and start to depolarize the ventricular myocardium early; when the normal impulse arrives through the His-Purkinje network, the rest of the QRS looks normal.
Potassium leaking from cells
Potassium shifts change the T wave and QRS width in hyperkalemia, not the upstroke as a delta wave.
set2.cite: 16. EKG Pericarditis Electrolytes and Other Abnormalities.pptx, Slide 27

set2.io: Topic — Preexcitation and accessory pathway tachycardias
set2.q: A 20-year-old man is told he has preexcitation. What does the term mean?
opts: Early ventricular activation via a bypass

Correct. Preexcitation is activation of the ventricles by a supraventricular impulse earlier than normal, through an accessory pathway that connects atria to ventricles and bypasses the atrioventricular node.
Delayed conduction in the bundle branches
Delayed bundle branch conduction is a bundle branch block; preexcitation is early activation through an accessory pathway.
Early repolarization of the epicardium
That describes benign early repolarization, a repolarization variant, not preexcitation.
Atrial firing faster than the sinus node
Preexcitation is about the route to the ventricles, not the atrial rate.
set2.cite: 16. EKG Pericarditis Electrolytes and Other Abnormalities.pptx, Slide 25

set2.io: Recognize ECG findings associated with: COPD/COLD, pulmonary embolism, hypothermia
set2.q: An 80-year-old woman with hypothermia has the 12-lead shown. Below which core temperature do these notched waves typically appear?
opts: Correct. As the temperature approaches 35°C (95°F) sinus bradycardia appears and the intervals then prolong; below 32°C (90°F) Osborn waves become apparent.
At about 35°C (95°F) the first change is sinus bradycardia; Osborn waves need cooling below 32°C (90°F).
That is normal body temperature, at which no hypothermic changes occur.
That is a fever. Osborn waves are a hypothermia sign, below 32°C (90°F).
set2.cite: 16. EKG Pericarditis Electrolytes and Other Abnormalities.pptx, Slide 16; tracing from Slide 17
set2.alt: Twelve-lead electrocardiogram on grid paper, with each lead labeled

set2.io: Compare and contrast ECG findings associated with: BER, acute pericarditis, STEMI patterns
set2.q: A 26-year-old man's 12-lead is shown, with coved ST elevation in V1 and V2. Which structure does his inherited disease affect?
opts: Left ventricular potassium channels
Brugada syndrome is a sodium channel disease of the right ventricular outflow tract.
An accessory atrioventricular pathway
An accessory pathway (bundle of Kent) causes Wolff-Parkinson-White preexcitation, with a short PR and delta wave, not coved V1 to V3 elevation.
The pericardial sac
Pericardial inflammation causes global concave ST elevation with PR depression, not right precordial coved elevation.
Right ventricular outflow sodium channels
Correct. Brugada syndrome is an inherited arrhythmogenic disease that affects the sodium channels of the right ventricle's outflow tract.
set2.cite: 16. EKG Pericarditis Electrolytes and Other Abnormalities.pptx, Slide 10; tracing from Slide 11
set2.alt: Twelve-lead electrocardiogram on grid paper, with each lead labeled

set2.io: Topic — Thyroid disorders
set2.q: A 61-year-old woman has a slow heart rate and the low-voltage 12-lead shown, with flattened T waves. Which endocrine disorder best fits it?
opts: Hyperthyroidism
Hyperthyroidism is a state of adrenergic hyperactivity; its commonest finding is sinus tachycardia, then atrial fibrillation.
Hypercalcemia
Hypercalcemia shortens the ST segment and QTc; it does not cause global low voltage.
Hyperkalemia
Hyperkalemia peaks the T wave; this tracing's T waves are flattened and its voltage is low.
Hypothyroidism
Correct. Hypothyroidism slows the metabolic rate and myocardial contractility: sinus bradycardia with global low-voltage QRS complexes, flattened or inverted T waves, a prolonged QTc and low P waves.
set2.cite: 16. EKG Pericarditis Electrolytes and Other Abnormalities.pptx, Slide 45
set2.alt: Twelve-lead electrocardiogram on grid paper, with each lead labeled

set2.io: Compare and contrast ECG manifestations of electrolyte abnormalities.
set2.q: A 59-year-old man with untreated kidney failure has the 12-lead shown: very wide QRS complexes, no P waves and peaked T waves. Without treatment, which pattern comes next?
opts: Prominent U waves
Prominent U waves are a hypokalemia sign, the opposite disturbance.
A shortened QT interval
A shortened QTc with the T wave against the QRS is the hypercalcemia pattern.
Osborn waves
Osborn waves are terminal QRS notches of hypothermia, not the end stage of hyperkalemia.
A sine wave
Correct. Hyperkalemia progresses from peaked T waves to flattened P waves and a wide QRS, and finally to a sine wave, the end-stage pattern.
set2.cite: 16. EKG Pericarditis Electrolytes and Other Abnormalities.pptx, Slide 34; tracing from Slide 36
set2.alt: Twelve-lead electrocardiogram on grid paper, with each lead labeled

set2.io: Topic — Preexcitation and accessory pathway tachycardias
set2.q: A 19-year-old man has occasional palpitations. His 12-lead in sinus rhythm is shown. Which pattern does it show?
opts: Left bundle branch block
A bundle branch block widens the QRS but leaves the PR interval normal and has no delta wave.
Wolff-Parkinson-White
Correct. A short PR interval, a slurred upstroke of the QRS (delta wave) and a widened QRS, the diagnostic triad, is Wolff-Parkinson-White preexcitation.
Ventricular paced rhythm
A paced rhythm has a pacing spike before each wide QRS, not a short PR interval with a slurred delta wave.
Brugada syndrome
Brugada changes are coved or saddleback ST elevation in V1 to V3, not a short PR with a delta wave.
set2.cite: 16. EKG Pericarditis Electrolytes and Other Abnormalities.pptx, Slide 28
set2.alt: Twelve-lead electrocardiogram on grid paper, with each lead labeled

set2.io: Compare and contrast ECG findings associated with: BER, acute pericarditis, STEMI patterns
set2.q: A 38-year-old man's tracing shows global concave ST elevation, but also ST depression in leads II and III. How should it be interpreted?
opts: Typical acute pericarditis
Pericarditis has no reciprocal ST depression outside aVR and V1; depression in II and III rules it out as the diagnosis.
Benign early repolarization
Early repolarization also has no reciprocal depression outside aVR and V1, so this depression argues against it too.
A normal variant in young men
Normal variant ST elevation is early repolarization, which has no reciprocal depression; depression here must raise an infarction.
Consider an acute infarction instead

Correct. If there is ST depression in any lead other than aVR and V1, or any Q waves in any lead, the tracing cannot be diagnosed as pericarditis and an acute ST-elevation infarction must be considered.
set2.cite: 16. EKG Pericarditis Electrolytes and Other Abnormalities.pptx, Slide 5

set2.io: Compare and contrast ECG findings associated with: BER, acute pericarditis, STEMI patterns
set2.q: A 74-year-old woman with chest pain has a left bundle branch block. Why are Sgarbossa's criteria needed?
opts: The block lowers the troponin
The criteria answer an electrocardiographic problem, the distorted ST segment, not a laboratory one.
The block itself distorts the ST segment

Correct. Left bundle branch blocks and ventricular paced rhythms cause global ST elevation, T-wave changes and wide QRS complexes, so ordinary criteria cannot locate an infarction; Sgarbossa's criteria are used instead.
The block makes the rate too fast
Rate is not the problem; the widened QRS with global ST and T changes is.
Standard leads cannot be placed
All twelve leads are recorded normally; it is the block's own ST and T changes that hide an infarction.
set2.cite: 16. EKG Pericarditis Electrolytes and Other Abnormalities.pptx, Slide 13
